# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardium. Once considered rare and untreatable, CA is now recognized as an underdiagnosed cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), aortic stenosis, and arrhythmia [1,2]. Advances in noninvasive imaging and the advent of disease-modifying therapies have transformed the diagnostic and therapeutic landscape [3].

## Types and Pathophysiology

More than 95% of CA cases are caused by either immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) amyloidosis or transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis [4]. AL amyloidosis arises from a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia producing misfolded light chains, which exert direct cardiotoxicity in addition to mechanical infiltration [5]. ATTR amyloidosis results from destabilization of the transthyretin tetramer, a hepatically synthesized transport protein for thyroxine and retinol. It occurs as a hereditary form (ATTRv) caused by pathogenic *TTR* variants, and as wild-type disease (ATTRwt), historically termed senile systemic amyloidosis, predominantly affecting older men [6,7]. The Val122Ile variant is notably prevalent among individuals of West African ancestry [8].

Amyloid deposition increases ventricular wall thickness and stiffness, producing a restrictive physiology with progressive diastolic and ultimately systolic dysfunction [9]. Microvascular involvement and autonomic dysfunction further contribute to the clinical syndrome.

## Clinical Presentation

CA should be suspected in patients with unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy, particularly with discordantly low electrocardiographic voltages [10]. Extracardiac "red flags" aid recognition: bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, spontaneous biceps tendon rupture, peripheral and autonomic neuropathy, and—in AL—periorbital purpura and macroglossia [11]. ATTR-CA frequently coexists with severe aortic stenosis, especially the low-flow, low-gradient phenotype, and is increasingly identified in HFpEF cohorts, where prevalence may reach 13% [12,13].

## Diagnosis

Diagnostic evaluation begins with screening for a monoclonal protein using serum and urine immunofixation and serum free light-chain assay; a normal panel makes AL highly unlikely [14]. Echocardiography typically reveals increased wall thickness, biatrial enlargement, and reduced global longitudinal strain with apical sparing ("cherry-on-top" pattern) [15]. Cardiac magnetic resonance demonstrates characteristic diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement and elevated native T1 and extracellular volume [16].

A pivotal advance is bone-avid radiotracer scintigraphy using ⁹⁹ᵐTc-pyrophosphate (PYP), DPD, or HMDP. Grade 2–3 myocardial uptake, in the absence of a monoclonal protein, permits a noninvasive diagnosis of ATTR-CA with high specificity, obviating endomyocardial biopsy in many cases [17,18]. When a plasma cell dyscrasia is present, tissue confirmation with mass spectrometry–based typing remains essential to avoid misclassification [19]. Genetic testing distinguishes ATTRv from ATTRwt and informs family screening [20].

## Prognosis

Untreated AL-CA carries the worst prognosis, with median survival of months when advanced cardiac involvement is present. Staging systems based on cardiac biomarkers (NT-proBNP, troponin) and the difference in free light chains stratify risk [21]. For ATTR-CA, staging using NT-proBNP and estimated glomerular filtration rate predicts outcomes [22]. Overall, early diagnosis is associated with improved survival across subtypes [23].

## Treatment

Management of AL-CA centers on rapidly suppressing the clonal plasma cells. Daratumumab-based regimens combined with bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone have improved hematologic and organ responses [24]. Autologous stem cell transplantation benefits selected fit patients.

For ATTR-CA, transthyretin stabilizers are foundational. Tafamidis reduced all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations in the ATTR-ACT trial and remains the best-established therapy [25]. Acoramidis, a high-affinity stabilizer, demonstrated benefit on a composite clinical outcome in the ATTRibute-CM trial [26]. Gene-silencing agents that reduce hepatic TTR production—patisiran (siRNA) and inotersen (antisense oligonucleotide)—were initially validated in hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy [27,28]. Vutrisiran, a subcutaneous siRNA, subsequently reduced mortality and cardiovascular events in patients with ATTR-CA in the HELIOS-B trial [29]. Emerging strategies include CRISPR-based in vivo gene editing and anti-amyloid antibodies designed to promote fibril clearance [30].

Supportive heart failure care emphasizes cautious diuresis; neurohormonal antagonists are often poorly tolerated owing to restrictive physiology and autonomic dysfunction. Anticoagulation is warranted for atrial arrhythmias given high thromboembolic risk, even in sinus rhythm with atrial mechanical dysfunction.

## Conclusion

Cardiac amyloidosis has evolved from an orphan diagnosis to a treatable condition. Heightened clinical suspicion, judicious use of biomarkers and scintigraphy, and accurate subtyping enable timely diagnosis, while stabilizers, silencers, and plasma-cell–directed therapies offer meaningful improvements in survival and quality of life. Future work will refine therapy sequencing, evaluate combination approaches, and pursue curative gene-based strategies.
